prize_parts.citation: for establishing modern political economics by analysing how constitutions, electoral rules and state capacity shape fiscal policy and public-goods provision

statement.case_for: After the exchange I keep B016 first, with moderate and reduced confidence. It is a mature programme of about three decades that gave economics a formal framework, backed by cross-country and within-country evidence, for how electoral rules, constitutional form, accountability and state capacity map into taxation, spending and public-goods provision. That is a first-order question for public economics and development, and it is taught and extended widely. The three-name cut is the clearest division of the specific contribution. Persson and Tabellini built the constitutions-and-policy framework. Besley, with Persson, built the political-agency and state-capacity strand. Alesina cannot be credited and Acemoglu and Robinson were recognised in 2024. I have narrowed the citation from round 1 to rules, state capacity, fiscal policy and public-goods provision. That wording follows the distinction several of us drew from the 2024 prize on the long-run historical origins of institutions. The case rests on the framework and on the later within-country designs it generated. It does not rest on any single cross-country coefficient.
statement.case_against: My central reservation is the one I would press hardest in my own field. Constitutions and electoral systems are not randomly assigned, and many of the cross-country estimates are correlational or rest on contested instruments. Next to the best design-based work on the list, the evidential side of B016 is weaker. Thematic proximity to the 2024 prize may still read as reduced marginal novelty, and a narrower citation lowers that risk without removing it. Credit between the Persson-Tabellini and Besley-Persson strands cannot be cleanly separated. The round-1 exchange sharpened two points against my own ranking. B001 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist. B020 has the widest footprint in data and estimation, which is the kind of contribution I normally value. My preference for B016 therefore rests on breadth and field-building more than on the strength of identification. Several of its supporters, myself included, share Stockholm-area or Swedish-institutional proximity to the field. The three first-choice files should not be read as three independent assessments.

responses.point: Hassler agrees that identification for constitutional effects is weaker than for design-based work and that the citation should emphasise the framework and research programme. He adds that his agreement with me should not count as independent evidence.
responses.response: I agree on all three points, and I have rewritten the citation along those lines. The framework is the strongest part of B016. Later within-country and subnational designs have sharpened it, but they do not make the early cross-country estimates causal. I also accept your caution about counting. We overlapped at Stockholm University in 2010-17 and we are close to the same field, so our shared first choice is weaker evidence than a count of two would suggest. The merit comparison with B001, B019 and B020 should rest on the arguments, and I have tried to set it out that way.

responses.point: Andersson keeps B016 behind B001 for three reasons: apportioning credit across three names, contested identification in constitutional comparisons, and thematic adjacency to the 2024 prize.
responses.response: Two of your three reasons I accept in substance. Identification is contested, and the Persson-Tabellini and Besley-Persson strands are not cleanly separable. On the 2024 overlap I still disagree, because the two prizes concern different objects. The 2024 work explains why countries differ in prosperity through the historical origins of institutions. B016 explains how rules inside contemporary political systems produce different fiscal outcomes. I also grant that B001's attribution advantage is real, and my confidence in B016 has dropped because of it. What keeps B016 ahead for me is that its contribution is wider and less entangled with other shortlist items, since Helpman's credit does not have to be allocated. I would not call that a decisive margin.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B001 first. He argues that the Grossman-Helpman models make sharper, more testable predictions than the constitutional comparisons in B016, and that his own closeness to B016's field makes him wary of overweighting it.
responses.response: The sharper-predictions point is fair and it is the strongest argument for B001 over B016 from my perspective. A model whose prediction can be put to data is better placed than a correlational constitutional comparison. Two things temper it. The mixed record of protection-for-sale tests, which you also acknowledge, means the sharpness has not translated into settled confirmation. Second, B016 has produced a broad empirical literature in public economics and development, even if its early identification was loose. I take your wariness about proximity as a model for how I should treat my own, since my closeness to B016 comes through the IIES macro-group overlap and not through any candidate. I regard B001 as my first alternative and not as a lesser one.

responses.point: Dreber argues that the China-shock papers are a joint Autor-Dorn-Hanson body of work, so omitting Dorn creates an attribution gap where credit is clearest. She agrees that Katz's overlap with already-recognised work weakens a Katz slot.
responses.response: You have moved me on Dorn. In round 1 I proposed only Autor and Hanson, on the grounds that the choice among Dorn, Katz and others was contested. If the China-shock evidence is the achievement being credited, Dorn belongs with it, because the core papers are joint and the credit is clearest there. If B019 were chosen, I would support Autor, Hanson and Dorn with a citation limited to trade-shock and technology adjustment evidence. I still do not think the task-framework strand fits within one citation without stitching two contributions together. I also still weigh the continuing debate over shift-share exposure measures and long-run persistence. That is why B019 stays an alternative for me and not my first choice, even though its best designs are the most credible on the list.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B020 first and B001 last of his eight. He argues that the selection and reallocation mechanisms have been confirmed against firm-level data in many countries, while protection-for-sale predictions have been confirmed less consistently.
responses.response: I did not rank B020 at the opening, and this exchange has shown me I should have weighed it more. Your empirical-confirmation argument is the kind that persuades me, and I take it seriously. The attribution gap you and Boppart identify, with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum outside the credited list, is the part that keeps me from moving it above B016. A Helpman-Melitz award would be defensible, and I could accept it if the Committee prefers a trade award. I would want the Scientific Background to describe the empirical precursors fully. I still read B001 and B020 as distinct achievements and would not combine them. Between the two I now think B020 has the stronger empirical case, and B001 has the cleaner credit.

uncertainties: Whether a citation limited to rules, state capacity and fiscal outcomes separates B016 from the 2024 institutions prize enough to remove the overlap concern.
Whether the Persson-Tabellini and Besley-Persson strands can be defended as one achievement under a three-name citation, given that Alesina (deceased) and Dixit are outside the set.

How much weight conceptual and field-building contribution should carry when the identification of the underlying causal claims is contested. This is the weighting that most separates my first choice from B019 and B020.

Whether B001's cleaner attribution or B020's wider empirical footprint should outrank B016 if the Committee decides to recognise trade. I would accept either as a single-part award, with B001 as my first alternative.
Whether the China-shock persistence and shift-share debates in B019 are settled enough for a citation. If so, whether Dorn or Katz is the third name. I now favour Dorn.
I have not independently verified citations or priority claims. My assessment rests on the supplied committee materials and my recollection of the literature.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Persson, Tabellini or Besley appears in my supplied profile, and none to the credited names on B001, B019 or B020. I was at Stockholm University in 2010-17 and overlapped with the IIES macro group (Hassler, Krusell). That is an institutional overlap and not a co-authorship, and I note that Hassler and Krusell also prefer B016. My long-standing Uppsala and IFAU co-authors (Holmlund, Edin, Åslund, Öckert, Johansson, Nybom) are not credited on any shortlisted item. Holmlund is also a frequent co-author of committee colleague Hjalmarsson, which is a tie between members and not a link to a candidate. My political-economy-adjacent and labour-economics interests are disclosed. Colleagues have flagged possible Swedish-institutional proximity of some B016 candidates to the Committee. I note that without adjudicating it or verifying any specific relationship.
